column2: On the authority of Abū ʿAbdillāh al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) say:

“The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters which many people do not know. Whoever guards against the doubtful matters has kept his religion and his honour free of blame;

and whoever falls into the doubtful matters falls into the unlawful, like the shepherd who grazes [his flock] around a sanctuary, about to graze in it. Indeed, every king has a sanctuary; indeed, the sanctuary of Allah is what He has made unlawful.

Indeed, in the body there is a lump of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart.” Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
His words, “The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters which many people do not know”, divide things into three categories:
First: the clearly lawful, such as grains, fruits and livestock, provided they do not reach a person by unlawful means.
Second: the clearly unlawful, such as drinking wine, eating carrion and marrying women within the prohibited degrees. These two categories are known to both the learned and the common people.
Third: the doubtful matters, which waver between lawful and unlawful, being neither clearly lawful nor clearly unlawful. Many people do not know these, though some do.

His words, “Whoever guards against the doubtful matters has kept his religion and his honour free of blame; and whoever falls into the doubtful matters falls into the unlawful, like the shepherd who grazes around a sanctuary, about to graze in it. Indeed, every king has a sanctuary;

indeed, the sanctuary of Allah is what He has made unlawful”, go back to the third category, the doubtful matters. A person should avoid them, for in that lies the safety of his religion in what is between him and Allah, and the safety of his honour in what is between him and people,
so they have no way to impugn his honour on that account. If he is careless about falling into doubtful matters, that may drag him into falling into the clearly unlawful.

The Prophet ﷺ gave the example of the shepherd grazing around a sanctuary: if he is far from the sanctuary, he is safe from his livestock straying into it, but if he is close to it, his livestock may well stray into it without his noticing.

What is meant by the sanctuary (ḥimā) is fertile land that kings and others protect, preventing others from approaching it; whoever grazes around it is about to fall into it, exposing himself to punishment.

The sanctuary of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is the unlawful things He has prohibited. A person must keep far away from them, and must also keep away from the doubtful matters that may lead to them.

His words, “Indeed, in the body there is a lump of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart”: muḍghah (“lump of flesh”) is
a piece of flesh the size of what one chews. This shows the great importance of the heart in the body: it is the king of the limbs, and they are sound when it is sound and corrupt when it is corrupt.
Al-Nawawī said: “His ﷺ words, ‘and whoever falls into the doubtful matters falls into the unlawful’, may carry two meanings:
First, that he falls into the unlawful while thinking it is not unlawful.
Second, that the meaning is that he has come close to falling into the unlawful, as it is said:
Sins are the messenger of disbelief,

because when the soul falls into disobedience it moves step by step from one evil to another greater than it. It has been said that this is what is alluded to in the saying of the Exalted: ‘…and they killed the prophets without right; that was because they disobeyed and were transgressing’ [Āl ʿImrān 3:112],

meaning that they progressed by sins until they killed the prophets. And in the hadith: ‘Allah has cursed the thief who steals an egg and has his hand cut off, and steals a rope and has his hand cut off’, that is, he progresses from the egg and the rope to [the kind of] theft [that carries the punishment].”

Al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr (may Allah be pleased with them both) was one of the younger Companions; he was eight years old when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died. In narrating this hadith he said, “I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say”,

which shows that a young child who has reached the age of discernment can validly receive [narrations], and that what he received when young and conveyed when grown is accepted. Likewise a disbeliever who received [a narration] while a disbeliever and conveyed it as a Muslim.
An explanation of the division of things in the Sharīʿah into the clearly lawful, the clearly unlawful, and the doubtful that wavers between them.
Many people do not know the doubtful, while some know its ruling with its proof.
Refraining from doing what is doubtful until its lawfulness is known.
Giving examples to establish abstract meanings by likening them to physical things.
When a person falls into doubtful matters, it becomes easy for him to fall into clear [prohibitions].
An explanation of the great importance of the heart, and that the limbs follow it, being sound when it is sound and corrupt when it is corrupt.
The corruption of the outward is evidence of the corruption of the inward.
Guarding against doubtful matters protects a person's religion from deficiency and his honour from blame and disparagement.
